cross_system.title: Cross-system signal: credit_card flow leading stock — origination headroom
cross_system.body: Credit card spending at shops (POS) is up 9.32 percent and online (e-commerce) is up 4.97 percent, but the actual credit card loans outstanding grew only 1.33 percent. ATM cash withdrawals on cards fell 1.0 percent. People are swiping cards more but not borrowing much more yet, which means there is room to lend.
cross_system.implication: The bank should push credit card loans now because customers are spending but loan balances have not caught up, so there is clear headroom to grow the book before demand cools.
chain: Customers are using their cards more for purchases at stores and online
The loan balances on those cards have barely grown, lagging far behind the spending increase
This gap means people have capacity and appetite to borrow more on cards right now

basis.headline: Credit card spend (value) (Payments) → Credit Card Outstanding (Credit): moving together
chain: Leading side: Credit card spend (value) (Payments) atm -1.0% · ecom +5.0% · other +2366.0% · pos +9.3% YoY.
Lagging side: Credit Card Outstanding (Credit) +1.3% YoY.
The two sides are moving together → this reads as origination headroom.

cross_system.title: Unsecured retail credit appetite — expanding (5/5 measurements observed)
cross_system.body: Personal loans for credit cards and other purposes grew 3.78 percent and 12.7 percent year-on-year, while credit card balances outstanding rose 8.15 percent. Consumer durable loans fell 3.38 percent. Most unsecured lending is expanding, meaning banks are willing to lend more to people without collateral because they see demand and acceptable risk.
cross_system.implication: A bank should grow its unsecured personal loan book now, especially in the other personal loan category growing at 12.7 percent, while watching credit quality closely since these loans have no asset backing.
chain: Banks are lending more personal loans without collateral, with growth of 3.78 percent and 12.7 percent in two categories
People are borrowing more on credit cards too, with outstanding balances up 8.15 percent, showing steady demand for unsecured credit
This is a good time to lend in these categories, but the bank must monitor repayment carefully because there is no property or gold to recover if borrowers default

basis.headline: Unsecured retail credit appetite → expanding
chain: Measured inputs: Credit Card Outstanding +1.3% YoY, Other Personal Loans +12.5% YoY, Consumer Durables -2.6% YoY, Credit card spend rising, Credit cards outstanding +8.5% YoY.
Member directions combine — measures and proxies count as-is, contra-indicators flipped — giving an expanding read on 5 of 5 measurements.

The willingness of households to carry — and lenders to extend — unsecured retail credit. No pipeline measures it directly: SIBC measures the unsecured stock (credit-card outstanding, other personal loans, consumer durables), payments measures the flow (credit-card spend) and reach (cards in force). Together they bound the construct: when stock, flow and reach move together the appetite read is unambiguous; when they diverge, the divergence itself is the signal.
Direction sustained across two composed periods → status active.

cross_system.title: Card-based consumption activity — expanding (5/5 measurements observed)
cross_system.body: Card terminals grew 1.45 percent, vehicle loans jumped 17.97 percent, but consumer durable loans fell 3.38 percent. People are borrowing heavily to buy cars and trucks, using cards a bit more, yet pulling back on financing fridges and TVs. The pattern says households are spending selectively—big-ticket transport yes, home goods no.
cross_system.implication: A bank should push auto finance hard, keep card offers steady, and avoid chasing consumer-durable portfolios until that 3.38 percent decline reverses.
chain: Card infrastructure is growing at 1.45 percent and vehicle lending is surging at 17.97 percent, so people are transacting more and financing expensive transport.
At the same time consumer durable lending dropped 3.38 percent, meaning households are skipping loans for appliances and electronics.
Banks should allocate capital to auto loans where demand is strong and wait on durable-goods credit until appetite returns.

basis.headline: Card-based consumption activity → expanding
chain: Measured inputs: Credit card spend rising, Debit card spend falling, POS terminals -0.5% YoY, Consumer Durables -2.6% YoY, Vehicle Loans +17.3% YoY.
Member directions combine — measures and proxies count as-is, contra-indicators flipped — giving an expanding read on 5 of 5 measurements.

Household consumption as expressed through card rails. Payments measures the transaction flows (credit + debit card spend) directly; acceptance infrastructure (POS terminals) proxies the merchant side of the same activity; SIBC's consumer-durable and vehicle loan stocks proxy the credit-financed share of it.
Direction sustained across two composed periods → status active.

cross_system.title: Unsecured spend–stock cycle — running (3/3 segments live)
cross_system.body: This is a feedback cycle read across both pipelines: spending, balances, and appetite feed each other. The basis below shows each segment and whether it is currently running with the cycle or against it.
cross_system.implication: A fully-running cycle compounds; a segment moving against it is the early warning that the cycle is turning. Watch the reversed segment.
chain: Segment states: Unsecured retail credit appetite → Credit card spend (value) — running; Credit card spend (value) → Credit Card Outstanding — running; Credit Card Outstanding → Unsecured retail credit appetite — running.
A loop fires only when every segment runs in its expected direction; 3 of 3 are live, so the cycle is running.

Appetite expresses as card spend (flow), spend accumulates into card balances (stock), and growing balances evidence the appetite that started the cycle. The loop fires only when all three segments move the same way — a clean composed read that the unsecured retail cycle is running (or, reversed, unwinding). Segments span both pipelines plus the confirmed flow→stock cross-edge.

sibc.title: Co-lending & warehouse-financing infrastructure
sibc.body: Small business credit is growing at 26.2% this year and now makes up 23.1% of all business lending. Growth in micro and small business loans jumped by 23.8pp because government systems like UDYAM registration and GST data now let lenders check if tiny businesses are real and can pay back. Banks cannot reach thousands of small borrowers alone, so they lend through partners who find customers and do the checking.
sibc.implication: A bank should set up deals with NBFCs and fintech partners to lend money for small business loans, using the new government data to decide who gets credit.
chain: Government created UDYAM registration and GST records that prove small businesses exist and show their sales
These records let lenders check if tiny borrowers can repay, so lending to micro and small businesses jumped by 23.8pp
Banks need local partners to find and check thousands of small borrowers, so they should lend through NBFCs who do that work
sibc._driver: MSME formalisation via UDYAM registration + GST data

sibc.title: Gold loan market entry / deepening for banks
sibc.body: Banks are growing gold loans by 105.5% compared to last year, and this growth has continued for 12 straight periods. Gold prices jumped sharply between 2023 and 2026, so customers can now borrow much more money using the same gold jewelry or coins as security. Banks are winning customers from finance companies because they have local branches where staff can check the gold is real and store it safely, plus they charge lower interest rates.
sibc.implication: Banks should open more gold loan counters in branches, train staff to test gold quickly, and advertise lower rates to pull customers away from finance companies while gold prices stay high.
chain: Gold prices rose sharply from 2023 to 2026, so the same gold jewelry is now worth more and customers can borrow bigger amounts against it
Banks have local branches with vaults and trained staff to verify and store gold safely, and they charge lower interest than finance companies, so customers are switching to banks
Banks should add more gold loan counters, speed up the testing process, and promote their lower rates to capture even more of this fast-growing market

sibc.title: MSME origination infrastructure investment window
sibc.body: Small business lending is growing at 32.7% per year, and these tiny businesses now make up 23.1% of all MSME lending. Their growth rate jumped by 23.8pp recently, while bigger MSME borrowers are growing much slower—the gap is 11.8pp. Banks can now check if these small businesses can repay loans using government registration systems and GST records, which makes lending safer and faster.
sibc.implication: Banks should invest in systems that connect to UDYAM registration and GST databases to quickly approve loans for small businesses, because these borrowers are growing fast and becoming easier to check.
chain: Small businesses are registering with the government and filing GST returns, creating digital records of their activity
Banks can now use these records to verify income and business health quickly, making it safer to lend to borrowers they couldn't check before
This opens up a fast-growing segment where demand is strong and competition is still light
sibc._driver: MSME formalisation via UDYAM registration + GST data

sibc.title: PLI anchor-supplier chain finance
sibc.body: The government is paying big manufacturers to build new factories under a scheme, and those manufacturers need more parts from smaller suppliers. Lending to suppliers in basic metals grew 22.6% and 18.4%, chemicals grew 22.6% and 21.8% and 14.2% and 7.4%, and engineering grew 23.9% and 38.3%. These suppliers are safer to lend to because they have signed contracts with large established companies that guarantee payment.
sibc.implication: Banks should lend to small and medium suppliers in metals, chemicals, and engineering who have confirmed orders from big manufacturers building new plants, because the contracts reduce the risk of non-payment.
chain: Government pays big manufacturers to build factories, so those manufacturers order more parts from smaller suppliers
Suppliers with confirmed orders from big companies are safer borrowers because the contracts guarantee they will get paid
Banks can lend more to these suppliers with lower risk, especially in metals, chemicals, and engineering where growth is fastest

sibc.title: PSLC market depth from PSL reclassification surplus
sibc.body: Housing loans that count toward priority sector lending jumped 39.0% in one year because RBI raised the ceiling in October 2024. Banks did not reclassify actual new lending—they simply moved existing housing loans into the priority bucket under the new rule. This creates instant surplus PSL credits that banks can sell to other banks who fall short of their required priority sector targets.
sibc.implication: The bank should buy PSL credits from banks with surplus housing-loan classifications if it is short on priority targets, or sell credits if it now has excess after reclassifying its own housing book.
chain: RBI raised the housing loan ceiling that counts for priority sector in October 2024
Banks moved existing housing loans into the priority bucket without lending more money, creating a 39.0% jump in reported priority housing loans
Banks with surplus credits can now sell them to banks that need to meet their priority sector targets
sibc._driver: RBI PSL housing loan ceiling revision (Oct 2024)

sibc.title: Renewable energy project finance — next capex wave
sibc.body: Old infrastructure lending is shrinking — some sectors fell -37.6% and -14.5% this year — while renewable energy sectors jumped 82.8% and 23.8%. Banks already have teams that know how to finance big, long-term projects like highways and power plants, and those same skills work for solar, wind, and green hydrogen projects.
sibc.implication: The bank should move project finance teams from old infrastructure to renewable energy, because government targets mean these new projects now need the same kind of big, long-term financing that old infrastructure used to get.
chain: Old infrastructure projects are finishing and paying back loans faster than new ones are starting, so lending in those sectors is falling
Renewable energy projects are growing fast because of government targets, and they need the same kind of long-term project financing
Banks can use their existing project finance skills and teams to lend to solar, wind, and green hydrogen instead of waiting for old infrastructure to recover
sibc._via: Project lifecycle phase → new origination vs repayment

sibc.title: Services sector credit entry / scale-up
sibc.body: Services sector lending is growing at 20.4% per year and now makes up 28.3% of all bank credit. Banks are lending more through NBFCs that serve services companies — this channel grew 19.7% and is getting stronger. Three services sub-sectors are growing extremely fast: one at 54.9%, another at 41.0%, and a third at 33.7% per year.
sibc.implication: Banks should build or expand partnerships with NBFCs that lend to fast-growing services sub-sectors, especially the three racing ahead at 54.9%, 41.0%, and 33.7%, to capture this 20.4% growth wave without taking all the direct risk.
chain: Services companies need more credit and the sector is growing at 20.4% yearly, now 28.3% of all bank loans
Banks are using NBFCs as a safer way to reach these borrowers, and that NBFC channel just grew 19.7%
Three specific services areas are exploding at 54.9%, 41.0%, and 33.7%, so banks lending through NBFCs to those pockets can grow fast while sharing the risk
sibc._driver: NBFC credit channel recovery post risk-weight cycle

sibc.title: EV-specific vehicle credit products
sibc.body: RETIRED at first FOUNDATION (2026-06-10). No external source verified for EV share of vehicle loans or EV-specific credit risk differentiation. No L1 signal separating EV from ICE vehicle loans. Returns only when EV share of vehicle loans is measurable in L1 (e.g., VAHAN registration data ingestion).
sibc.implication: Move on this while the trend is still running in your favour.

sibc.title: Infrastructure repayment wave with insufficient new origination pipeline
sibc.body: Banks over-indexed to traditional infrastructure credit face a structural squeeze: the FY22-24 project book moves to repayment (compressing balances) while the next-cycle pipeline (renewables, data centres) is slower to ramp. Banks without next-cycle project finance capability face credit portfolio contraction.
sibc.implication: Move on this while the trend is still running in your favour.
chain: As a project cohort moves from construction (drawdown) to operations (repayment), net credit balance declines unless new origination offsets it — suppressing growth even while existing books remain large.
This is being driven by Infrastructure supercycle completing (FY22–24).
sibc._via: Project lifecycle phase → new origination vs repayment

sibc.title: CIC reporting compliance gaps creating off-balance-sheet credit risk
sibc.body: RBI Digital Lending Guidelines (2022/2025) require BNPL and digital credit to report to Credit Information Companies. However, compliance may be incomplete among newer digital lenders operating under first-loss guarantee structures or co-lending arrangements where the regulated entity's on-book exposure is partially shielded. If reporting gaps exist, the true unsecured credit stress is understated in bank balance sheets and in SIBC data.
sibc.implication: Move on this while the trend is still running in your favour.
chain: Higher risk weights raise the regulatory capital cost per unit of exposure, compressing origination economics for unsecured retail products until reversed.
This is being driven by RBI risk-weight hike on unsecured credit (Nov 2023).
sibc._driver: RBI risk-weight hike on unsecured credit (Nov 2023)
sibc._via: Regulatory capital weight → unsecured origination economics

atm_pos.title: Credit card penetration deepening — PSB share gap is the opening
atm_pos.body: India has 12.0 crore credit cards growing at 8.5% a year. Private banks hold 70.9% of all credit cards, while public sector banks hold only 23.8%. Public banks control about 64% of debit cards, which means they already have millions of customers who could be offered credit cards at much lower cost than finding completely new customers.
atm_pos.implication: Public sector banks should offer credit cards to their existing debit card customers, because they already know these people and trust them enough to give them debit cards, so the cost of getting a new credit card customer is very low.
chain: Private banks have 70.9% of credit cards but public banks have most of the debit cards in the country
Public banks already have a relationship with these debit card holders and know their banking behavior
Public banks can offer credit cards to these existing customers at very low cost compared to finding brand new customers

atm_pos.title: Rural cash distribution via Micro ATM / Business Correspondent networks
atm_pos.body: India has 13.6 lakh micro ATMs that let villagers withdraw cash without visiting a full branch, but the number fell -8.1% recently. These machines are closing or fewer are being added even though people in small towns still need cash every day. A micro ATM costs far less to run than opening a real branch.
atm_pos.implication: A bank should keep or add micro ATMs in villages where branches are too expensive, because villagers still need cash and these machines are cheap to operate.
chain: The count of micro ATMs dropped -8.1% so fewer machines are available in villages
Villagers still need cash daily but full branches cost too much to build and staff
Banks can serve these customers cheaply by keeping micro ATMs running instead of closing them

atm_pos.title: Embedded transit and tap-to-pay payment products
atm_pos.body: Credit card spending in the 'other' category jumped 2366.0% in value and 714.0% in volume year-on-year. Millions of people are now tapping cards at metro gates, vending machines, and small shops that just installed tap-to-pay terminals. This is not existing cardholders spending more — it is people using cards in completely new places for the first time.
atm_pos.implication: Banks should issue cards to people who ride the metro or shop at small stores, because these customers will start using cards for everyday purchases once the terminals are in place.
chain: Metro gates and small shops install tap-to-pay terminals
People who never used cards before start tapping to pay for rides and snacks
These new users keep the card in their wallet and begin using it for other purchases too
atm_pos._driver: Embedded card payment infrastructure rollout (transit NFC or RuPay-credit-on-UPI)
atm_pos._via: Embedded payment rails → new card-spend surface

atm_pos.title: Credit card market concentrated in top-5 private banks
atm_pos.body: The top-5 private banks control approximately 71% of credit card outstanding. The largest single issuer holds ~20% of the market. This concentration creates systemic fragility — as demonstrated when a single payment bank's exit caused a market-wide debit card step-down. Similar disruption from a major credit card issuer would have proportionally larger effects.
atm_pos.implication: Move on this while the trend is still running in your favour.

atm_pos.title: Debit card base structural decline reducing cash access for underbanked
atm_pos.body: The debit card base is contracting through payment bank exits and lifecycle purges. This reduces the potential transaction base for populations that depend on debit cards for cash access and digital payments — particularly lower-income and rural segments without credit cards or reliable UPI-linked accounts.
atm_pos.implication: Move on this while the trend is still running in your favour.
chain: Regulatory wind-down of a major issuer forces cancellation of its entire card portfolio, producing a single-period step-down in the stock concentrated in that issuer's lender category.
This is being driven by RBI enforcement action against Paytm Payments Bank (Jan–Apr 2026).
atm_pos._driver: RBI enforcement action against Paytm Payments Bank (Jan–Apr 2026)

atm_pos.title: Payment acceptance bifurcation: POS contracting while UPI grows
atm_pos.body: POS terminal network contraction while UPI QR expands creates an acceptance gap: merchants who drop POS terminals cannot accept international cards, EMI transactions, premium credit card features, or POS-authenticated payments. Customers without UPI-linked accounts face reduced options at merchants who have switched fully to UPI.
atm_pos.implication: Move on this while the trend is still running in your favour.
chain: Zero MDR on UPI makes QR acceptance structurally cheaper than card POS (no hardware, no per-txn fee), driving QR deployment while suppressing POS-terminal investment. Polarity is per-target: + for QR, − for POS.
This is being driven by Zero MDR policy on UPI transactions (NPCI/GoI).
atm_pos._driver: Zero MDR policy on UPI transactions (NPCI/GoI)
